@graph.name: Deposit Silk
@graph.description: From the artist: "This performance experimented with livecoding audio, using FM synthesis, modulating sinewaves and sawtooth waves. I used euclidean rhythms which created clashes and unfamiliar patterns in the sound. Sampling pop-cultural references and internet one-liners behave as my vocals for my sound usually. The livecoding of the audio and visuals is done through Strudel.cc, this performance mixed ambient sound and noise together. Usually, I look to my livecoding peers for reference, sometimes remixing their code, I am a fan of open-source and community knowledge sharing."
@graph.keywords: performance art, experimental performance, London

@graph.name: Lagtime Seedling
@graph.description: Lagtime Seedling scores and performs audio-visual compositions made entirely within web browser windows using a large number of live youtube.com video tabs. Through a meticulously choreographed way of using their laptop, they create narrative and musical journeys through strange and overlooked corners of the web. Transparency and accessibility is central to their practice: Lagtime Seedling doesn't use any traditional music software. Instead, all their sound comes from youtube tabs and a piano keyboard on a separate virtualpiano.net browser window. They interact with their browser as anyone could, using keyboard shortcuts to navigate many tabs and windows quickly, and interact with videos through youtube's default hotkeys. The sound and visuals of lagtime's compositions, being pulled straight from youtube, carry on a certain algorithmic qualia. Full of ASMR, slime squishing, nail scratching, and soft spoken words, their compositions reflect the overstimulating experience of being online. Through a carefully arranged score, lagtime recontextualises online content, extracting overlooked emotion embedded within it.
@graph.keywords: browser performance, audio-visual, live coding, YouTube, internet art, ASMR

@graph.name: Slow Impulse
@graph.label: Performance Night

images.alt: Poster for slow impulse night

@graph.description: Slow Impulse, an experimental sound night, was the final closing event of our festival Can We Start Again? and moved through six sets that each pulled sound from unexpected places. Ellis Berwick and Willow Swan opened with their sculptural, industrial instruments, setting a tone that was as much about materials as music. The London Community Laptop Orchestra followed, creating a communal space within the stage for people to play and interact with their laptops and phones before settling into a slower stretch of harmonizing healing frequencies. Genia Isachenko then took over with a rig of amplifiers, speakers and an old radio, weaving vocals through static and interference. Lagtime Seedling and Rosemary Moss played a double youtube duet across two projectors on either side of the large school hall. Conscript Theatre's Elia Fielden and Emile Belli reworked fragments of 'Untitled Robot Story,' folding writing about military machinery, memory and love into sound. Finally, the night closed with a full concerto of phones and alarms, guitars, cello and piano alongside ringtones and clocks.
@graph.previewDescription: A six act experimental performance night delving into sounds from unusual sources, emanating throughout a large school hall to close off our festival <<Can We Start Again?

@graph.name: Spiral: the shape of cultural temporality & protocol-art
@graph.label: Talk

images.alt: Documentation from the Spiral talk at Phreaking Collective's Can We Start Again? exhibition, London, 2026 — photo 1 of 3
Documentation from the Spiral talk at Phreaking Collective's Can We Start Again? exhibition, London, 2026 — photo 2 of 3
Documentation from the Spiral talk at Phreaking Collective's Can We Start Again? exhibition, London, 2026 — photo 3 of 3

@graph.description: Atay Ilgun, a London-based artist, creative technologist, and curator whose work bridges AI, web3, event curation, and experimental art, drew on his practice across early AI, crypto, and protocol art to think through cultural time and the hype cycle, using the spiral as a form that reads emergence and obsolescence together. He proposed network and protocol art as work that operates from inside its own infrastructure, holding its prior states forward as material rather than breaking from market-dependent digital culture — a reality hack from within it. The talk moved through Otherness and the ./spiral exhibition, co-curated with jonooo on SuperRare, alongside soft world, his curatorial studio for protocol art, examining hypercycles, crypto, and alternative paths toward a quieter, more durable version of what digital culture could still become.

@graph.name: Nina Davies
@graph.label: Talk
@graph.description: Speed Running the World of Things. As part of this programme Nina Dvies opens up her research in progress, presenting it as a fragmented talk. Opening with teenagers speedrunning a Scientology building, she traces a series of tangents through Boston Dynamics' dancing robots, NASA's 'riding the skin' VR experiments, and the world models that teach physical AI to rehearse being in our world before it arrives. Drawing on several years of research into what happens to human movement when it leaves the body, the talk arrives at a single question: as physical AI inherits human movement to navigate a human-built world, what new forms of embodied literacy must we develop to navigate it in return?

@graph.label: Workshop

images.alt: Documentation from the Worldbuilding as Resistance workshop at Phreaking Collective's Can We Start Again? exhibition, London, 2026 — photo 1 of 3

@graph.description: Ameer Ali and Ericka Simon, founders of LiBi, led this hands-on workshop using their browser-based worldbuilding engine to explore its potential for creating sovereign 3D spaces. Participants worked at a personal scale, using their own assets or ready-made models to shape rooms and small landscapes and personalise them with lighting, atmosphere, audio, and detail, framing worldbuilding as an act of resistance against corporate platforms and surveillance. By the end of the session, participants had a standalone 3D world shareable through the web, alongside foundational skills for building interactive experiences going forward.

@graph.description: Olivia Ema, a lecturer at University of the Arts London, digital artist, and founder of a creative technology studio, spoke as a Black woman working in creative technology about how identity and intuition shape the systems and worlds she builds. She walked through how digital systems built in software like Touchdesigner could hold presence, respond to a room, and shift something in people almost without them noticing, drawing on her own projects — an interactive floor installation reflecting on grief, and large-scale installations across London from Outernet to Piccadilly. The talk moved through both the technical process behind the work and what was actually driving it underneath, staying grounded in theory and critical awareness throughout.

@graph.description: Sophie Nadel led a hands-on workshop teaching participants how to translate an address, password, or secret phrase into a hidden code and embroider it onto their belongings, drawing on her design system supported by the Data Reclamation Handbook. The practice encouraged storing information offline, away from prying data collection, while offering a slow, meditative approach to data sovereignty that recentred embroidery as a craft historically dismissed as "women's work." Participants brought their own items to embroider, with needles, scissors, and materials provided.

@graph.description: Kat Macdonald, a London-based sound and performance artist exploring collective practice, desire, and public space through technology and performance, led participants through the history of ringtone customization and the politics of sound in the commons. Using RTTTL, the Ring Tone Text Transfer Language developed by Nokia in 1996 to make and share ringtones between early mobile phones, participants made and shared their own custom ringtones, centering ideas around the politics of sound in public space.

@graph.description: Data artist and UAL Associate Lecturer Tiziana Alocci asked what happens to everything digital systems cannot measure as they optimise for speed, extraction, prediction, and surveillance, arguing that the absence of data often matters more than what gets recorded. @graph.name: Hear how you look, see how you sound
@graph.description: 'Hear how you look, see how you sound' is a self-eroding portrait booth that turns every visitor's image into sound, invites them to “play” that sound, then burns the edited audio back into the picture's pixel data. Each cycle bruises the file a little more, leaving behind a corrupted photographs that audibly and visually catalogue the show's slow decay. The piece literalises data's tendency to drift, break and disappear once it leaves our hard drives and circulates in public space.

@graph.name: Subtle Crisis
@graph.description: Subtle Crisis is an interactive audiovisual work that translates personal social anxiety into a form of digital decay. A serene point‐cloud landscape opens the piece, drawn from 3‐D scans of spaces in which I once felt safe. A live microphone continuously samples the gallery's ambience—footsteps, murmurs, coughs, unforeseen clatters. Each sonic fragment is analysed in real time; its amplitude and spectral “noise” values become parameters that fracture the point‐cloud in subtle increments: vertices blur, drift, or vanish outright, as if corrupted sectors were blooming across the image.

images.alt: Subtle Crisis

@graph.name: Internet Checkpoints
@graph.description: Internet Checkpoints is a reflection on the fragments of the web that live outside of visibility. Broken links, forgotten pages and digital traces that no longer serve the logic of the algorithm. Rooted in the idea of Legacy Russell's glitch as digital resistance, an error that shifts outside the expected flow, the work draws from a specific kind of online artefact: intentional uploads with no proper name, blank titles, usernames made of symbols, and nostalgic game landscape footage shared without explanation. These artefacts often float without context, designed to evade recognition, to appear only through luck or misdirection and often unreachable again.

@graph.name: Master in training
@graph.description: Centring on a physical still life, the artist's traditional gymnasium, this installation exposes the absurdity of generative AI. Triggered by a button, the system captures reality but refuses to see it, replacing the objects with "perfect" statistical fabrications that immediately melt into digital entropy. As the image degrades, the system attempts to make sense of the noise, searching the Flickr archive for human memories that match its own distorted visions.

@graph.name: I live there with you
@graph.description: A poem based sculpture, drawn unease when struggling to remember something, as is often the case, and couldn't, as I had no signal. I had instinctively reached for access to the cloud, with the realisation that all my memories are stored online, on data centres I'll never see, physically owned by someone else is an unnerving feeling of loss. Knowing these memories I struggle to recall, are amalgamating into reasoning models, is there's a fraction of yourself in them? Elements of the poem will creep in but are purposefully obscured instead, focusing on the mental imagery.

@graph.name: Window
@graph.description: Window activates a global architecture to forge a hole through a wall. Utilising Apple's Facetime video call infrastructure, Window employs a connection between two devices spaced 30cm apart made by passing data to the Wifi router, over copper cables to a local exchange, fibre optics to the Internet Service Provider's core network, onto the London Internet Exchange, to Apple Edge Servers in a London datacentre, and all the way back again. In cutting a virtual hole in the wall, Window stretches the interior space of the gallery around a city.

@graph.name: Precipitation Network
@graph.description: Precipitation Network is an installation that materialises network infrastructure through live environmental signals and renders network activity as a dynamic physical condition. The system measures local network activity, including Wi-Fi traffic, device presence and ambient signal activity, and maps these variables to physical outputs such as light, mist, and motion. Viewers and their devices continuously influence the system, modulating its behaviour in real time and foregrounding their participation in normally imperceptible infrastructures.

@graph.name: i potato self-portrait
@graph.description: i potato self-portrait is a durational generative portrait of a potato. The fidelity of the portrait is controlled by the health and charge of a large potato battery array. It runs a custom image diffusion model trained on a dataset of 10,117 images of healthy, and diseased potatoes. The voltage of this potato battery controls the health of the generated potatoes. As the potatoes dry up and lose the ability to generate power, so does the health of the potato in the portrait. Eventually, i potato self-portrait will no longer be able to produce an image of a healthy potato.

@graph.name: recursive_wait
@graph.description: recursive_wait is a computational performance in which client-server communication becomes a metaphor for persistence without resolution. A minimal network-one browser client, one server-loops endlessly. The client sends requests; the server never delivers. Each failure returns an error carrying a single poetic line. Over time, these fragments accumulate in the browser's developer console, forming a poem that is never identical and never complete. On screen, a cockroach circles a white plate like a loading spinner-an homage to Tarkovsky's The Sacrifice. Around the monitor, tangled network cables form a nest of connectivity that leads nowhere. The work offers no interaction. Meaning does not arrive as an answer, but slowly assembles through waiting.
